name: Glama
summary: The largest public directory of MCP servers, which builds and runs each open-source server in a Firecracker sandbox to record its tools, score their descriptions and flag risky behavior, plus hosting and a gateway for the servers you use.
intro: Glama lists about 97,600 open-source MCP servers and 30,400 remote connectors, with some 985,000 tools between them, and re-publishes everything in the official MCP Registry. A maintainer claims a listing by signing in with GitHub and proving write access to the repository. Glama then clones the repository, builds it from its Dockerfile (or one its build system infers), and runs it in a throwaway Firecracker microVM. Inside, it asks the server for its tools, resources and prompts and stores their full JSON schemas, while watching system calls and network traffic for things like reads of SSH keys or traffic to hosts the code never mentions. Servers that fail to build stay hidden from search, and every new commit triggers a rescan; Glama says it ran over a million scans in a year.

Each tool description gets a Tool Definition Quality Score across six dimensions (purpose, usage guidelines, side effects, parameters, conciseness and completeness), and remote connectors are re-introspected on a schedule, with schema changes diffed and checked for prompt injection. The results are public on each listing and through a REST API.

Around the directory Glama sells the pieces for running servers: one-click hosting on dedicated machines, a gateway that sits between clients and any MCP server to manage OAuth tokens, allow or block single tools and log every JSON-RPC message, and a browser-based MCP inspector. Glama also runs a chat workspace and an AI gateway for model providers; in April 2026 it open-sourced the gateway’s core as Lightport, limited the hosted gateway to a curated set of providers and said it was going all-in on MCP.
strengths: Breadth: about 97,600 servers and 30,400 connectors, a superset of the official MCP Registry
Evidence instead of a bare listing: captured tool schemas, sandbox behavior findings, quality scores and change history for each server
A machine-readable API (with an OpenAPI description) and per-server config snippets for Cursor, Claude Desktop, Claude Code and VS Code
One vendor for finding, testing, hosting and gating servers, with call logs and per-tool access control in the gateway
limits: Directory API reads need an API key, and the data license requires visible attribution to Glama and a link to each record’s listing wherever you show it
Scans are automated heuristics: Glama keeps its detection rules partly private, and a clean listing is not a security review of your own deployment
Prices for hosting, the gateway and chat are behind sign-up rather than on a public pricing page
The pipeline is built and maintained by Frank Fiegel and contributors, and the directory competes with copycat sites and with the free official MCP Registry

story: Anthropic published the Model Context Protocol in November 2024, and within days Glama’s blog ran an MCP quickstart by the author punkpeye (25 November), who also started the awesome-mcp-servers list on GitHub (30 November). The list, which links to Glama’s directory and its Discord, has since passed 96,000 stars on GitHub.

A list of links could not say whether a server worked or was safe, so Glama turned the directory into a registry: build every server from source in a sandbox, record what it actually exposes, and watch what it does. By late 2025 punkpeye wrote of a year of constant iteration on the directory, and of finding it copied page for page by a competitor. By 2026 Glama re-published everything in the official MCP Registry alongside its own findings, and in April it published its Tool Definition Quality Score as open source.

Glama had also run a chat workspace and an AI gateway in front of dozens of model providers. In April 2026 it open-sourced that gateway as Lightport, cut the hosted gateway down to a curated set of providers and pointed users to OpenRouter for the rest, saying it was going “all-in on the MCP ecosystem”.

choices.choice: Build and run every server instead of trusting its README
choices.why: Introspecting a running server gives the real tool schemas, and running it in a fresh Firecracker microVM lets Glama watch for credential access or unexpected network traffic without exposing shared infrastructure.

choices.choice: Score tool descriptions, not just servers
choices.why: Models choose tools from their descriptions; research Glama cites found well-described tools were selected far more often and that most public tools had at least one defect, so each listing shows a per-tool score with fixes.

choices.choice: Be a superset of the official registry
choices.why: The MCP steering group’s registry holds vendor-neutral metadata only, so Glama ingests all of it and layers its sandbox findings, scores and change history on top.

choices.choice: A gateway rather than a thin proxy
choices.why: Teams running many servers need OAuth handled, tools enabled one by one and every call logged, which a pass-through proxy does not do.
